Alypius
a-lĭp´ĭ-ŭs
n. (Alypius of Thagaste, d. c. 430, Augustine's closest friend, baptized with him at Milan in 387 and afterward bishop of Thagaste)
Latin form of the Greek alypios, ‘free from grief.’ Known to the church almost entirely through Books VI and VIII of Augustine's Confessions.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Alypius was Augustine's younger townsman and pupil, and the Confessions tell his story as a case study in how habit masters a decent man. At Carthage he was enslaved to the circus races and was cured by a chance remark in one of Augustine's lectures. At Rome, dragged by friends to the gladiatorial show, he kept his eyes shut until a roar of the crowd opened them; he looked, drank in the savagery, and went home a lover of blood. Paul's warning describes the mechanism exactly: “evil communications corrupt good manners” (1Co 15:33). Yet the same man refused a bribe as a legal assessor when the powerful pressed him. In the garden at Milan he took up the book after Augustine had read it, found the next words, “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye” (Rom 14:1), applied them to himself, and followed his friend into the faith without delay. He was baptized with Augustine by Ambrose at Easter 387 and later served as bishop of Thagaste. His life commends the friendship of Proverbs: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines friend as one who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem and respect which lead him to desire his company and seek to promote his happiness.

FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection.

2. One not hostile; one who is on the same side.

3. A favourer; one who is propitious; as, a friend to virtue.

Key Scripture

Rom 14:1 — "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations."

Rom 13:14 — "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof."

1Co 15:33 — "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners."

Pro 27:17 — "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend."

Modern Corruption

Alypius is remembered as a minor character in someone else's conversion, which misses the point the Confessions make with him: the eye is a door, and a good man can be taken through it in a single afternoon.

expand to see more

Modern readers treat Alypius's fall at the arena as quaint — a scrupulous young man upset by a violent spectacle. Augustine treats it as a demonstration of the doctrine of sin. Alypius trusted his own resolve (absent in mind, he boasted, he would overcome both them and the show), and the boast was the beginning of the defeat. Our entertainment culture runs on the same confidence: that a man can watch anything, because watching is not doing. The Scriptures never grant the premise; they guard the eye because the eye feeds the heart.

The corrective is not withdrawal from all company but the right company. Alypius was dragged down by friends and lifted up by a friend. The church has always needed both warnings: “evil communications corrupt good manners” (1Co 15:33), and, in the other direction, a brother who will read the next verse to you and take it as meant for himself. The recovery is ordinary Christian friendship — men who keep one another out of the arena and bring one another to the Word.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek homilia (G3657), companionship, communication; proslambano (G4355), to receive, take to oneself; Hebrew re'a (H7453), friend, companion.

Greek homilia (G3657) — company, communication; 1 Corinthians 15:33, the only New Testament use.

Greek proslambano (G4355) — to receive, take to oneself; Romans 14:1, 15:7.

Hebrew re'a (H7453) — friend, companion, neighbour; Proverbs 17:17, 27:17.

Usage

"“Him that is weak in the faith receive ye” (Rom 14:1) — the verse Alypius took for his own in the garden at Milan."

"“evil communications corrupt good manners” (1Co 15:33) — the lesson of the arena at Rome."

"“Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17) — the friendship that brought him to the font."
